summary: Fine-tuning makes sense when you need to change a model's behavior, tone, or output format consistently, or teach it specialized tasks that prompting alone can't reliably enforce. RAG is the better choice when you need up-to-date or proprietary knowledge retrieval without baking facts into weights, and prompt engineering should always be tried first for cheap, fast iteration. In practice, teams reach for fine-tuning after prompting and RAG plateau on accuracy, latency, or cost at scale.
when_to_fine_tune: Choose fine-tuning when you need consistent structured outputs, a specific tone/style, or classification behavior that prompting cannot reliably reproduce across inputs.
Use fine-tuning (not RAG) when the task requires learning a skill or reasoning pattern rather than retrieving facts, since RAG injects knowledge but doesn't change model behavior.
Fine-tune to reduce token/latency costs by shrinking long few-shot prompts into learned weights, improving throughput at production scale.
Prefer fine-tuning a smaller open model over a large general one when you want lower inference cost and ownership for a narrow, high-volume domain task.
